Use Latin forms only in limited situations – for example:

in technical and specialist publications that use them.
Use the English words where possible

If you think you need to include ‘etc.’ because there’s more to say, include these ideas in your sentence instead.

rules.quote: Avoid using Latin shortened forms in most content
rules.specification: The page gives examples of permitted special-use contexts rather than an exhaustive definition. Whether another context warrants Latin needs judgement. The specific instruction against ‘etc.’ is unqualified.
rules.violation_condition: A Latin shortened form appears instead of English without an applicable special-use context, or ‘etc.’ is used despite the specific instruction against it.
when: Latin forms are permitted where space is limited, such as in tables.
Latin forms are permitted in technical and specialist publications that use them.
Other special-use contexts may qualify; the listed situations are examples.
The preference for ‘for example’ and ‘that is’ over ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’ is particularly relevant in more formal publications.
The page specifically says not to use ‘etc.’ and identifies its redundancy after ‘for example’, ‘such as’ or ‘including’.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the general avoidance instruction and its named applications; retain special-use exceptions and the specific treatment of ‘etc.’ without producing overlapping findings.

rules.quote: The terms ‘i.e.’ and ‘e.g.’ need full stops after each letter.
rules.violation_condition: An occurrence of the Latin shortened form ‘i.e.’ or ‘e.g.’ lacks a full stop after either letter.
when: Applies when either shortened form is used, including in contexts where Latin forms are permitted.
rules.why: G-4: the body sentence states the actionable punctuation requirement; the screen-reader explanation is not another rule.

rules.quote: Don’t follow ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ with a comma, regardless of whether you would use a comma in the sentence.
when: Applies even when the sentence would otherwise take a comma at that position.
rules.why: G-2: the instruction explicitly rules out a sentence-based exception; this is distinct from both abbreviation avoidance and missing full stops.
